h: Raphael, a mechanical tiger and a very big bed
p: A few objects here have real 'you have to see this' status. Tipu's Tiger is an 18th-century wooden automaton of a tiger mauling a European soldier, built for Tipu Sultan of Mysore, and it even had a little organ inside to make growling and wailing noises. It's strange, grisly and fascinating, and it sparks great conversations about empire and how objects end up in museums.

Then there's the Great Bed of Ware, an enormous carved Elizabethan four-poster so famous that Shakespeare mentions it in Twelfth Night. Over in the Raphael Court, huge designs for tapestries by Raphael, known as the Raphael Cartoons, fill an entire room, and the Ardabil Carpet, one of the most celebrated Persian carpets anywhere, is shown in low light to protect its colours.

Fashion fans should head for the circular fashion gallery, which traces centuries of what people wore, from stiff corsets to catwalk showpieces. The jewellery galleries sparkle away upstairs, and the photography displays are a good change of pace if your feet need a slower amble.

Pick two or three areas and give yourself around two hours; the building is a maze of corridors and staircases, so grab a map and expect to get happily lost at least once. The garden courtyard café is a welcome pit stop when your feet start to protest, and it's a lovely place to regroup before round two. If you've got very young children, it's worth knowing about Young V&A in Bethnal Green, a sister museum designed especially for kids and families, which makes a great separate day out. Back in South Ken, the Exhibition Road Cultural Quarter, the Royal Albert Hall and Hyde Park are all on the doorstep.
